authored.title: Thammasat (dhammasattha)
authored.body_html:
What this is

The thammasat (ธรรมศาสตร์; Pali dhammasattha) is the cosmic law-treatise — the text that tells a Southeast Asian legal world where law comes from and why it binds. Its defining claim is startling if you take it literally, and the tradition means it literally: law is not made. It is older than kings, older than the world's present inhabitants, and it was found — read off the boundary-wall at the edge of the universe by a sage who went and looked.

It is the kadi tham pole of law — the dhamma-law — standing above and legitimating the king's enforceable code, the Mangraisat. A Lanna judge worked between the two.

The story, first — law read off the wall of the world

Tradition holds — the following is the narrative frame of the wider Mon–Burmese–Tai dhammasattha literature, not established from the twenty witnesses catalogued below. Treat it as orienting.

The origin story starts before there is anything to have law about. In the Buddhist cosmology the treatises assume, the world dissolves and reforms in enormous cycles, and the beings who repopulate it after each dissolution begin as luminous, self-illuminating, weightless, without sex, hunger, or property. Then one of them tastes the sweet earth-crust that has formed on the water. The taste is the beginning of everything that follows: eating makes bodies coarse, coarse bodies cast shadows and need shelter, difference appears, appetite appears, and then — the moment the treatises are really about — someone takes rice from a plot that another had marked as theirs. The first theft in the history of the world. And because there is no procedure, the injured party can do nothing but strike back.

So the beings assemble and elect the first king, the Mahāsammata, "the Great Elect" — chosen by agreement to judge between them, paid a share of the rice for doing it. Tradition holds the office begins as a contract, not a conquest: the first monarch is a hired arbitrator.

But the king still has the problem of by what standard. And here the sage enters. In the tellings, a seer of enormous attainment — named Manu in most recensions, a minister or counsellor to the first king — travels to the edge of the cosmos, to the great cakkavāḷa wall that encircles the world-system, and finds the law already written there in letters the size of full-grown cattle. He does not compose it. He copies it down, or memorises it, and carries it back for humankind.

Inference — every consequence that matters follows from that single image. If the law is inscribed on the wall of the universe, then a king who rules against it is not making bad law — he is misreading, which is a different and more dangerous kind of failure. The treatise arms the judge with a standard his own ruler cannot rewrite. That is not a decorative myth; it is the constitutional move of the whole tradition, and it is why the law shelf in this collection keeps the cosmological book right next to the enforceable one.

Tradition holds the recensions differ on the sage's fate, and one strand is worth recording for its honesty: in some tellings Manu, having delivered the law, judges a case wrongly himself — and the error is visible, in some versions to the point that he resigns or is unmasked. A legal literature that builds a fallible transmitter into its own founding story is telling its users something about how far to trust any single judgment.

What the catalogue holds

Twenty witnesses carry a thammasat / dhammasat name, nearly all classed as customary law. Set beside the twenty-four Mangraisat witnesses, the catalogue holds both poles of the Thai legal cosmos in near-equal number — a genuinely valuable pairing.

The cluster sorts into a few named recensions, and the names are informative:

  • ธัมมสาดหลวง Thammasat luang, "the great thammasat" — the full recension, at Wat Chiang Man in Chiang Mai (ms 803) and twice at Wat Lom Raed in Lampang (ms 4005, dated 1817; ms 4015, dated 1895) — the same house copying it afresh nearly eighty years apart.
  • ธัมมสาตรอม Thammasat hom — hom meaning gathered or compiled: an abridgement or digest (ms 4006 at Wat San Rim Ping, Lamphun, dated 1855; ms 4287). Alongside it ms 4475 at Wat Nantharam pairs วิไนรอม ธัมมสาด — the Vinaya digest and the thammasat in one title.
  • ธัมมสาดคดีโลกคดีธัมม Thammasat kadi lok kadi tham — the treatise presented explicitly as covering both poles at once (ms 4012 at Wat Ban Ueam, Lampang, dated 1841; ms 5033 from the same temple, dated 1947, a century later and classed canonical rather than law).
  • ธัมมสาสตร์ราชสาสตร์ Thammasat rachasat (ms 2031 at Wat Sung Men) — the dhamma-treatise and the king's treatise named as a matched pair, which is the whole architecture compressed into one title.

The hinge title

One witness holds the entire structure in a single line. ms 232, from Wat Phra That Chang Kham in Nan and dated 1852, is catalogued as คดีโลกคดีธัมม์ มังรายธัมมสาษ — Kadi lok kadi tham manglai thammasat: worldly cases, dhamma cases, Mangrai, thammasat. The two poles and the founder-king's name, bound together on one bundle of palm-leaf. And its cataloguers classed it not as law at all but as Buddhist canonical.

Inference — that classification is not an error to correct; it is evidence. A scribe in Nan in 1852 did not experience the cosmic frame and the king's code as two genres that happened to be adjacent. He experienced them as one subject, close enough to scripture that a cataloguer reading the bundle reached for the canonical shelf. This single shelf-mark does more to demonstrate the kadi lok / kadi tham architecture than any amount of description, because nobody constructed it to make the point.

Where it sits

The twenty witnesses spread Lampang 5, Chiang Mai 5, Phrae 3, Phayao 3, Lamphun 2 — with dated copies running 1817 to 1947. Inference — two things follow. First, the thammasat is a lowland-valley text: it clusters in the old müang capitals with established monastic schools, and it is thinner in Nan than the Mangrai law is, where the pattern reverses. The frame stayed near the centres of learning while the enforceable code travelled to the peripheries that needed it. Second, the 1947 copy is worth pausing on — a treatise grounding law in a sage's reading of the cosmic wall was still being hand-copied onto palm-leaf in a Lampang monastery two years after the Second World War ended.

Inference — that the two clusters are of comparable size is itself a finding: this collection preserves the whole legal architecture, not just its enforceable half. The thammasat supplies the theory, the Mangraisat the practice. Having both is what lets the archive show law as the tradition itself understood it — a single structure with a heavenly frame and an earthly body.

The regional inheritance

Tradition holds — the dhammasattha is not a Thai invention. The literature runs across the Mon, Burmese and Tai worlds, and the older strata are Mon-Burmese; the Lanna thammasat is the northern Thai branch of a trans-regional legal literature, which is part of why it recurs in so many copies and why its recensions vary. The name and the wall-of-the-world image are ultimately borrowed from the Sanskritic dharmaśāstra tradition — but the borrowing is thorough rather than faithful. Tradition holds the Buddhist recensions strip out the brahmanical caste ordering that organises the Indian originals and re-found the whole treatise on the Mahāsammata contract instead: law legitimated by an assembly's agreement rather than by birth. A borrowed frame, rebuilt around a different theory of where authority begins.

Notes

  • A well-attested anchor, best read as a pair. The hard facts are n = 20 and its near-parity with the Mangraisat's n = 24. The cosmological narrative above is marked tradition throughout; the cluster, the recension names, the provincial spread and ms 232 are catalogue data.
  • No page-level text yet. As with the whole law genre, none of the twenty has a transcribed page here — the Manu narrative is told from the wider tradition, not from these leaves. Transcribing one Thammasat luang would let this page quote its own witnesses instead.
  • Next move — the two-pole comparison. Inference — the highest-value pass is reading the thammasat and Mangraisat witnesses against each other, surfacing how the discovered-law frame and the king's-law code cite and depend on one another inside this one collection. ms 232, ms 2031 and ms 2032 — where both names share a title — are the natural starting points.
  • Read alongside. The king whose code this frame legitimates is Mangrai; the maxims a ruler was advised by, rather than bound by, are the Lokanīti. Browse the shelf at Customary Law.
